blocks.text: A garage-door header is made by nailing three planks together into an I-shape instead of milling a single solid beam. When the header is loaded, the flanges try to slide along the web, and the nails are the only thing stopping that slide. How many nails, and how far apart, depends on a quantity called shear flow.

blocks.markdown: In a beam built from several pieces, the longitudinal shear stress that exists at any interface (see the shear stress formula) must be carried across that interface by glue, nails, screws, bolts or welds. Rather than a stress, it is convenient to work with the **shear flow**: the shear force transmitted per unit length of the beam along the interface.

blocks.title: Shear flow
blocks.text: The **shear flow** $q$ is the horizontal shear force per unit length (N/mm or kN/m) that must be resisted along a longitudinal cut. Using the shear stress formula, $q=\tau\,t=VQ/I$, where $Q$ is the first moment, about the neutral axis of the whole section, of the area lying on one side of the cut.

blocks.caption: $s$ = maximum spacing of fasteners along the beam (mm) if each fastener (or row of fasteners at one cross-section) can resist a shear force $F_{\text{fast}}$ (N); $q$ in N/mm.

blocks.markdown: **Why shear flow and not shear stress?** A connector is a discrete device that carries a *force*. Between two successive fasteners a length $s$ of interface must be held, and the longitudinal shear force on that length is $q\,s$. Connectors must therefore be sized and spaced so that $F_{\text{fast}}\ge q\,s$. The thickness $t$ does not matter to the connector, only the total force per unit length passing through the interface.

blocks.title: Nails in a built-up I-beam
blocks.prompt: A beam is made of three planks nailed together: top and bottom flanges 150 mm wide by 30 mm thick, and a web 30 mm thick by 200 mm tall (overall depth 260 mm). It carries a shear force of 8 kN. Each nail resists 1.8 kN in shear, and one nail is placed at each cross-section where the flange joins the web. Find the shear flow at the flange-web interface and the nail spacing.

steps.text: Second moment of area of the whole section.
First moment of the top flange about the neutral axis (centroid 130 - 15 = 115 mm above it).
Spacing for a nail capacity of 1800 N.

blocks.answer: The shear flow is 29.6 N/mm, so nails must be at most about 60 mm apart (round down, for example 60 mm).

rows: Shear force diagram at the section
Using maximum V everywhere without noting it varies
Second moment of the whole section about its centroid
Area on one side of the interface times centroid distance to the section's neutral axis
Measuring distance from the flange's own centroid
Number of rows crossing the interface
Forgetting there are two interfaces in a box or double-web section

blocks.title: Screws in a T-beam
blocks.prompt: Two boards are screwed together to form a T-beam: a flange 200 mm wide by 30 mm thick above a web 40 mm wide by 180 mm tall. The shear force is 15 kN and each screw resists 1.2 kN. Find q and the spacing of screws.

steps.text: Centroid from the bottom: flange (6000 mm^2 at 195 mm) and web (7200 mm^2 at 90 mm).
Second moment of area by the parallel-axis theorem.
Flange first moment about the neutral axis (flange centroid 57.3 mm above it).

blocks.answer: q is about 92 N/mm and screws would need to be about 13 mm apart, which is impractical: a bigger fastener, glue or a different section would be selected.

blocks.title: Spacing may vary along the beam
blocks.text: Because $q=VQ/I$ is proportional to $V$, the required spacing is smallest where the shear force is largest (near supports) and can be relaxed toward mid-span. Designers often use two or three spacing zones along the beam.

blocks.title: Count the interfaces
blocks.text: In a box beam there are two joints on each flange (one at each web), so each carries half of the flange's $q$. A fastener must be capable of resisting force in shear at the interface, and the formula assumes fasteners behave rigidly with no slip.

points: Shear flow q = VQ/I is the longitudinal shear force per unit length at an interface, with Q the first moment of the area on one side of the interface about the whole section's neutral axis.
Connectors resist force, so the quantity they must carry is q multiplied by their spacing: s = F_fastener/q.
q is proportional to V; spacing can increase where the shear force decreases, and the number of interfaces carrying q must be counted.

questions.stem: What are the SI-compatible units of shear flow?

options.text: Force per unit length, such as N/mm
Force per unit area, such as MPa
Force times length, such as N mm

questions.correctOptionText: Force per unit length, such as N/mm

distractorRationale.a: Correct: q = VQ/I has units N x mm^3/mm^4 = N/mm.
distractorRationale.b: This is the unit of shear stress, which also uses the width t.
distractorRationale.c: This is a moment, not q.
distractorRationale.d: q is a force per length.

questions.explanation: Substituting V in N, Q in mm^3 and I in mm^4 gives q in N/mm. It is a force per unit length of beam, which is what a row of fasteners must resist.

questions.stem: A built-up beam's fasteners are spaced s apart. Why must they be designed for the shear flow q rather than the shear stress tau?

options.text: Shear stress is zero at an interface
Shear flow is a measure of bending moment
Each fastener must carry the force q x s from a length of interface, and a connector resists force, not stress

questions.correctOptionText: Each fastener must carry the force q x s from a length of interface, and a connector resists force, not stress

distractorRationale.a: Shear stress is non-zero at interfaces; it is q/t.
distractorRationale.b: q is force per length, not moment.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the longitudinal shear on length s is q s.
distractorRationale.d: Nails and bolts are mainly loaded in shear in this application.

questions.explanation: A fastener has no knowledge of the thickness t; it must transmit the total longitudinal force acting on its tributary length, equal to q multiplied by s.

questions.stem: For a built-up beam, the applied shear force V is doubled while fasteners and section remain the same. The maximum allowable fastener spacing then becomes:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: q doubles, so s = F/q halves.
distractorRationale.b: Inverted: more shear flow requires closer fasteners.
distractorRationale.d: Spacing depends on V through q.

questions.explanation: q = VQ/I is proportional to V, and s = F_fast/q, so doubling V halves the permissible spacing.

questions.stem: When calculating Q for the flange-web interface of an I-shaped built-up beam, the distance multiplying the flange area is measured from:

options.text: The centroid of the flange to the interface
The top of the flange to the neutral axis
The neutral axis of the whole section to the centroid of the flange

questions.correctOptionText: The neutral axis of the whole section to the centroid of the flange

distractorRationale.a: This gives the flange's own contribution, which is not the first moment about the NA.
distractorRationale.b: Not the centroid of the area, so it gives the wrong lever arm.
distractorRationale.c: Not a reference for bending stress distribution.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: Q = A' y-bar' about the neutral axis of the whole section.

questions.explanation: Q is the first moment about the neutral axis of the entire cross-section. The flange area is multiplied by the distance from that axis to the flange centroid.

questions.stem: True or false: if each fastener can carry a larger shear force, they may be spaced further apart for the same shear flow.
questions.explanation: Since s = F_fast/q, a bigger F_fast allows a proportionally bigger s. The shear flow is fixed by V, Q and I.

questions.stem: At a section of a built-up beam V = 20 kN, I = 1.6 x 10^8 mm^4 and the first moment of the flange about the neutral axis is Q = 4.0 x 10^5 mm^3. Find the shear flow at the flange-web joint in N/mm.
The shear flow at an interface of a built-up timber beam is 40 N/mm. Two nails cross the interface at each spacing, and each nail resists 1.6 kN in shear. Find the maximum nail spacing in mm.
questions.explanation: Force capacity per cross-section is 2 x 1600 = 3200 N. s = 3200/40 = 80 mm.

questions.stem: A box beam has top and bottom flanges 200 mm wide by 30 mm thick and two vertical webs, each 30 mm thick and 180 mm tall, with overall depth 240 mm. The shear force is 18 kN. The top flange is attached to each web by a line of screws, and each screw resists 2.0 kN. Find the maximum screw spacing in mm along each web-flange joint.
Explain why the connectors in a built-up beam must resist the shear flow VQ/I, and describe what Q represents for the joint between a flange and the web.
markingGuide: Defines shear flow as longitudinal shear force per unit length
Explains that bending stresses on two faces of a slice differ, producing a net longitudinal force on the flange portion
Connectors transmit force over their tributary length: F = q s
Q is the first moment of the area of the part attached by the joint (the flange) about the neutral axis of the whole section
Notes that without connectors the parts would slip and act as separate beams
questions.explanation: Connectors must supply the longitudinal force that would otherwise cause the layers to slide. That force per unit length is VQ/I, and Q is defined by what lies on one side of the joint.

questions.stem: A built-up beam under a uniformly distributed load has fasteners at a constant spacing designed for the maximum shear force. Explain how you could use fewer fasteners, and give two practical considerations that limit how widely they may be spaced.
markingGuide: Shear flow is proportional to V, which is largest at the supports and decreases to zero at mid-span for a uniform load
Required spacing s = F/q can therefore increase toward mid-span
Use zoned spacing (several spacings) rather than a single worst-case value
Limit: minimum edge/end distances and practical minimum spacing of fasteners
Limit: maximum spacing to prevent separation or buckling of flange between fasteners, and any code-prescribed limits
questions.explanation: Because q = VQ/I follows the shear force diagram, the demand on fasteners is not uniform. Matching the spacing to V saves fasteners but practical detailing rules still bound the spacing.
